>> Good morning. My name is Amoris Gomez
and I am the landlord engagement manager
for the office of homeless services.
Thank you for the opportunity to speak
to you today. I will be presenting on
the Metro Rapid Response Fund Pilot,
also known as MURF. I know there are a
lot of questions around it, so hopefully
my very lengthy presentation answers
some of that for you.
The um
so [clears throat] again, MetroRapid
Response, also known as MURF, is
designed to strengthen our homelessness
response system through the diversion
approach that helps individuals and
families access housing more quickly
before their homelessness becomes
prolonged and more difficult to resolve.
There is a there was a conversation, I
know, with the executive committee and
the suggestions that were made have been
considered and incorporated within the
MURF document. So, thank you. The
purpose of MURF is to address a gap in
our current housing system. Many HUDF
funded homelessness programs prioritize
individuals experiencing chronic
homelessness, often with those
co-occurring conditions. While this
prioritization is necessary, it can
leave individuals and families who are
newly homeless without timely access to
housing resources. Households who may
not score highly on the vulnerability
assessment often remain on housing list
for an extended period even though they
are still at a significant risk of
prolonged homelessness. So MURF creates
a local pathway that provides assistance
sooner, helping prevent short-term
housing crisis from beginning from
becoming long-term homelessness
situations.
And the goal of MURF is very simple.
that is to move into housing faster and
test whether earlier intervention leads
to a stronger long-term outcome and
prevent the return to homelessness. By
preparing short-term rental assistance,
I'm sorry, by pairing short-term rental
assistance with intensive case
management that is provided by our
community partners. MURF shortens the
time households spend unhoused, reduce
exposure to trauma associated with
homelessness, creates a pathway toward
long-term housing stability, and
prevents the return to homelessness.
This pilot allows us to evaluate whether
earlier investment improves long-term
outcomes for households and strengthens
the overall homelessness response
system.
Now, all individuals that are referred
to MURF must be considered housing
ready, meaning that they have the
essential documents and income needed to
secure and sustain permanent housing
using a targeted universalism approach.
The specific subop currently prioritized
in this p pilot include people
experiencing unsheltered homelessness,
families in emergency shelters, and
veterans experiencing literal
homelessness. These groups have been a
continued focus within our community.
However, some households may not score
high enough on the coordinated entry
assessment to quickly receive referrals
for housing programs. Households that
are housing ready are most likely to
benefit from the short-term assistance
and successfully uh be remade housed.
MURF provides a flexible financial
assistance to address immediate barriers
that prevent households from securing
housing. Financial assistance includes
rental aars, security deposits, first
month's rent, ongoing rental subsidies,
and utility assistance. By addressing
these financial needs quickly, we are
able to help households access housing
faster and be stabilized more quickly.
Because MURF is a pilot, uh at the
moment, we are focused on measuring
outcomes directly tied to financial
assistance.
This allows us to evaluate what is
working based on our local investment.
We access housing. I'm sorry. We assess
housing stability by looking at whether
the participants are moving into housing
and achieving stability faster,
achieving self-sufficiency and paying
rent, assessing other long-term rental
uh subsidies, and remaining hous and
avoiding return to homelessness.
Uh research on the rapid rehousing and
diversion focused interventions
consistently show that financial
assistance reduces the return to
homelessness and lowers long-term costs
in the broader system.
Once again, we are continuing to
evaluate the outcomes and refine the
approach as we learn what strategies are
most effective.
We do not yet have all the answers and
we are hopeful that this pilot will
provide a valuable insight. Now at this
time we cannot project a deadline for
when the pilot will become complete
um as uh ongoing evaluation is essential
to understand the long-term
effectiveness. Currently, OHS has
received 91 MURF referrals and of those
40 households have been successful in
securing housing and 51 are actively
working with OS staff and case managers
to identify housing, complete lease
applications, and overcome barriers
within their placement.
At this time, the referrals are made
through OHS street outreach teams,
emergency family shelters, and the
Department of Veteran Affairs. What
makes this pilot different is that it
introduces an alternative local
prioritization pathway. As I previously
mentioned, this allows Metro to serve
households who may not score high enough
for HUDf funed programs, but will still
be provided with immediate housing
intervention.
This diversion strategy creates
flexibility for Metro to address
barriers that contribute to longer stays
in homelessness and provide financial
assistance that prevent the return to
homelessness. By helping individuals and
families move into sustainable housing
more quickly, the demand for emergency
assistance decreases. This helps relieve
pressure across the homeless response
system, including coordinated entries,
emergency shelters, and other metro
departments.
Now, in closing, the Metro Rapid
Response Fund pilot provides a flexible,
locally responsive tool that allows us
to assist in assist households earlier
before their homelessness becomes
prolonged. By removing the immediate
financial barriers and providing
targeted support, MURF helps households
secure stable housing faster and
strengthens the overall effectiveness in
our homelessness response system. We are
hopeful that this pilot will provide
meaningful insight into how early
intervention can improve long-term
housing outcomes. Thank you.
